scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: A module often has test code at the bottom. Today we learn how to stop it running every time someone imports the file.

scenes.onScreen: "Run or imported?": three numbered lines (1. Python sets __name__ for every file; 2. A file run directly has __name__ equal to "__main__"; 3. An imported file has its own file name instead) and an analogy card: a shop with a front counter and a storeroom: the demo runs only when the shop is opened directly, not when someone borrows a tool
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: When Python runs a file, it sets a special name called dunder name. If you run the file directly, dunder name is the text, dunder main. If another file imports it, dunder name is the module's own name. So you can put an if at the bottom, if dunder name equals dunder main. Code under that if runs only when the file is run directly, not when it is imported.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] Import our module. Python runs shape dot py from top to bottom. It defines area, and then reaches the guard. Dunder name is shape here, not main, so the test line is skipped. [HL 2] Use the module's function. Twenty. [HL 3] The module's name is simply shape. If you run shape dot py directly, you see its test print instead.

The name is the module's own name, the guard is False, and the test is skipped. One file, two behaviours, chosen by one if.

Four: Put test or demo code under the main guard. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: test code runs on import
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Our module prints a test line at the top level. We import it, and the test line appears in our own program's output. Every top level line of a module runs when it is imported. Wrap the test in the main guard, and now it runs only when you run the module directly.

props.why: Every line at the top level of a module runs when it is imported, so a stray print appears in every program that imports it; guard it with if __name__ == "__main__".

scenes.onScreen: Why was the module so well behaved? It knew when it was main, and when it was only a guest.

shorts.title: What is __name__?
shorts.hook: "Every Python file has a special name called dunder name."
shorts.script: Every Python file has a special name called dunder name. If you run the file directly, dunder name is the text, dunder main. If another file imports it, dunder name is the file's own name instead. It is Python's way of telling the file how it is being used. One small value, and a very useful trick. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: How was I started?

shorts.title: The main guard
shorts.hook: "Put this at the bottom of a module."
shorts.script: Put this at the bottom of a module. If dunder name equals dunder main, colon. Everything below it runs only when you run the file directly. When another file imports it, the guard is False, and the code is skipped. It is the standard way to keep test code and demos in a module. The files that import it do not run them. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Run only when main.

shorts.title: Reusable code
shorts.hook: "Modules let you split a big program into small files."
shorts.script: Modules let you split a big program into small files. Put your functions in one file, and import them everywhere. Every file only needs to know the names it uses. If you fix a function once, every file that imports it gets the fix. That is why professional code is split into modules, and not written as one huge file. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Split into files.

shorts.title: Surprise output
shorts.script: A bug that confuses beginners. You import a module, and extra lines appear in your output. The module has print statements at the top level, and every top level line runs on import. Wrap test code in the main guard, and it only runs when you run the module itself. Your imports become quiet, and predictable. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Hide the demo.
